newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Lumumba declares support for Zairean rebels.
newsitem.headline: Lumumba declares support for Zairean rebels.

text.p: The son of Zaire's assassinated first prime minister Patrice Lumumba surfaced in Geneva on Thursday to declare his support for Tutsi-dominated rebels fighting to topple long-time ruler Mobutu Sese Seko.

Francois Lumumba told reporters he would travel to the eastern Zairean town of Goma on Monday to meet rebel leader Laurent Kabila and offer his support for the armed struggle to depose the cancer-stricken Mobutu.

"We congratulate Kabila and his forces for their courage in their armed struggle. We affirm our solidarity with the rebels. Their struggle is our struggle," Lumumba, 45, told a news conference, also attended by Zairean exiles in Switzerland.

Lumumba's father, assassinated in 1961, is a symbol of liberation throughout Africa and a national hero and political reference for many in Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL).

Lumumba said little about his underground opposition group and it is unclear what he has to offer Kabila, whose troops have captured half of Zaire and appear poised to end Mobutu's 31-year-old grip on power.
Asked what took him so long to declare support for the winning side, Lumumba merely said he always felt solidarity with the rebels but admitted he had not spoken to Kabila for months.
The "Lumumbists" are among exiled Zairean opposition groups that have been emerging to take advantage of the military gains of the rebels.

Kabila, who has opposed Mobutu since joining a rebellion in 1965 just after independence, was a comrade-in-arms in the 1960s of Marxist guerrilla Che Guevara and the roots of his ideology lie in the leftist nationalism of Patrice Lumumba.

Lumumba said Zairean opposition groups, including the recently ousted prime minister Etienne Tshisekedi who has been temporarily sidelined by the Kabila-Mobutu power struggle, should be part of any transitional power arrangement.

When pressed, he said he did not fully agree with Kabila on how to restore democracy: "Kabila has an important role to play in the transitional period. But we have differences of opinion. If he bans political parties, it would be a big error."
